title: Signals and Systems, MIT 6.003, Fall 2011 — shard 3: Sessions 14–19, Problem Sets 8–10, and Quiz 3
access: full (official MIT OpenCourseWare lecture notes, assignments, solutions, and assessment; course package metadata identifies the materials as CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, subject to separate third-party rights notices)
topics: Session 14 — Fourier Representations: periodic signals as sums of harmonics; CT Fourier-series analysis and synthesis; orthogonality; square- and triangle-wave spectra; Gibbs overshoot; LTI filtering of harmonics
Session 15 — Fourier Series: Fourier coefficients as orthogonal projections; musical and speech spectra; source–filter model of vowel production; formants; pitch-dependent intelligibility

Session 16 — Fourier Transform: passage from a periodic extension to an aperiodic CT signal; CTFT analysis and synthesis; relation to the Laplace transform; transform properties; scaling, duality, impulses, and periodic line spectra

Session 17 — Discrete-Time Frequency Representations: DT frequency response on the unit circle; pole–zero vector diagrams; conjugate symmetry; 2π periodicity and aliases; DT Fourier-series basis and coefficient formulas

Session 18 — DT Fourier Representations: all-pass phase effects; DTFS matrix form; radix-2 FFT decomposition and scaling; DTFT derivation as N→∞; relation to the Z transform; magnitude/phase experiments on images

Session 19 — Relations among Fourier Representations: unified CTFS, CTFT, DTFS, and DTFT table; periodic extension as frequency sampling; time sampling as spectral periodization; CT/DT frequency-variable relation Ω=ωT
Problem Set 8 — Direct and inverse CT Fourier series; coefficient matching by symmetry and support; deciding whether input/output pairs can be LTI; Gibbs overshoot and averaged partial sums

Problem Set 9 — Fourier series versus transform samples; duality; transform properties and pairs; Parseval's theorem; energy-retaining lowpass design; separating magnitude and phase effects of an RC filter

Problem Set 10 — DT Fourier series and inverse series; filtering periodic impulses; dual transform pairs; reconstruction from transform magnitude and phase; matching transformed signals to magnitude/angle plots

Quiz 3 — CT Fourier transform from a Laplace transform; DT pole–zero frequency responses; ideal DT lowpass impulse response; periodic input filtering; extracting echo delays and amplitude from measured frequency response
key_results: A CT signal with period T can be synthesized as x(t)=Σ_k a_k e^{j2πkt/T}; orthogonality gives the analysis coefficients a_k=(1/T)∫_T x(t)e^{−j2πkt/T}dt. The complex conjugate in the inner product is what sifts out one harmonic. [Sessions 14–15, slides 16–31 and 3–10]

Only periodic signals can be assembled from harmonics sharing one fundamental frequency. Fourier representation separates waveform shape into harmonic amplitudes and phases, making musical timbre and filtering visible in a common language. [Session 14, slides 3–15]

The unit square wave has a_k=1/(jπk) for odd k and zero for even k, while the corresponding triangle-wave coefficients are −1/(2π²k²) for odd k and zero for even k. A jump produces 1/k decay; one additional degree of smoothness produces 1/k² decay. [Session 14, slides 28–39]

Differentiation multiplies the kth CTFS coefficient by j(2π/T)k; integration therefore divides nonzero harmonics by that factor and requires the DC term to be handled separately. [Session 14, slides 34–38; Problem Set 8, Problem 1 and solution]

Near a jump, ordinary Fourier partial sums retain an approximately 9% limiting overshoot even as more terms narrow the ringing region. Averaging the first N partial sums removes the overshoot in the assigned sawtooth experiment and yields much smoother convergence. [Session 14, slides 39–41; Problem Set 8, Problem 5 and solution]

Complex exponentials are eigenfunctions of an LTI system: each input harmonic is multiplied by H(jkω0). An LTI filter changes only the amplitude and phase of existing harmonics and cannot create new frequencies absent from the input. [Session 14, slides 42–50]

A Fourier coefficient is an orthogonal projection under ⟨a,b⟩=(1/T)∫_T a*(t)b(t)dt, directly analogous to resolving a spatial vector into perpendicular coordinate components. [Session 15, slides 3–10]

The speech-production model factors a quasi-periodic glottal source from the vocal-tract filter. Vowels with similar pitch differ primarily through formant resonances; as sung pitch rises, sparse source harmonics sample those resonances less reliably and vowel identity weakens. [Session 15, slides 11–35]

Letting the period T of a periodic extension tend to infinity sends harmonic spacing ω0=2π/T to zero and converts the CTFS synthesis sum into an integral. The resulting pair is X(jω)=∫_{−∞}^{∞}x(t)e^{−jωt}dt and x(t)=(1/2π)∫_{−∞}^{∞}X(jω)e^{jωt}dω. [Session 16, slides 3–15]

If the bilateral Laplace ROC includes the jω axis, the CT Fourier transform is the Laplace transform evaluated at s=jω. The Fourier transform may exist when no Laplace ROC exists, as for a constant or eternal sinusoid represented by impulses in frequency. [Session 16, slides 16–19 and 32–36]

The CTFT inherits linearity, time shift, time scaling, differentiation, multiplication by t, and convolution properties from the Laplace transform. In particular, x(at)↔|a|^{−1}X(jω/a), so stretching in time compresses frequency while preserving spectral area. [Session 16, slides 20–29]
Transform values encode moments: X(0)=∫x(t)dt, and x(0)=(1/2π)∫X(jω)dω when inversion applies. These provide quick normalization checks for proposed transform pairs. [Session 16, slides 27–29]

Duality states that f(t)↔g(ω) implies g(t)↔2πf(−ω). It links a rectangular spectrum to a sinc in time and yields 1/(1+t²)↔πe^{−|ω|} from e^{−|t|}↔2/(1+ω²). [Session 16, slides 30–34; Problem Set 10, Problem 4 and solution]

Canonical generalized-function pairs include δ(t)↔1, 1↔2πδ(ω), δ(t−T)↔e^{−jωT}, and e^{−jω0t}↔2πδ(ω+ω0). A CT periodic signal has a Fourier transform consisting of impulses of area 2πa_k at its harmonic frequencies. [Session 16, slides 32–39; Session 19, slides 6–8]

For a rational DT system, pole–zero vectors evaluated at z=e^{jΩ} give the frequency response magnitude as a product of vector lengths and phase as the signed sum of vector angles. CT evaluates H(s) on the imaginary axis; DT evaluates H(z) on the unit circle. [Session 17, slides 10–28]
For real h[n], H(e^{−jΩ})=H*(e^{jΩ}). Consequently an eternal cosine at Ω emerges with amplitude |H(e^{jΩ})| and phase shift ∠H(e^{jΩ}). [Session 17, slides 14–17]

DT frequency is periodic modulo 2π because e^{j(Ω+2πk)n}=e^{jΩn}. Real cosine frequencies fold about π, so π is the highest distinct DT angular frequency and sampling can reverse intuitive CT frequency order. [Session 17, slides 29–42]

A DT signal periodic in N has exactly N distinct harmonic exponentials, the Nth roots of unity. Its DTFS pair is a_k=(1/N)Σ_{n∈⟨N⟩}x[n]e^{−jk2πn/N} and x[n]=Σ_{k∈⟨N⟩}a_ke^{jk2πn/N}; both x[n] and a_k are periodic in N. [Session 17, slides 45–53]

The DTFS analysis and synthesis matrices are scaled conjugates and inverses. Direct evaluation requires order N² multiplications, which motivates exploiting repeated roots of unity. [Sessions 17–18, slides 48–53 and 17–20]

A radix-2 FFT splits an N-point transform into transforms of the even and odd indexed samples, then combines them with twiddle factors. The recurrence M(N)=2M(N/2)+N gives M(N)=N log₂N multiplications rather than N². [Session 18, slides 19–32]

An aperiodic DT signal is the limit of periodic extensions as N→∞. The DTFT pair is X(e^{jΩ})=Σ_{n=−∞}^{∞}x[n]e^{−jΩn} and x[n]=(1/2π)∫ over any 2π interval X(e^{jΩ})e^{jΩn}dΩ. [Session 18, slides 33–38]

If a sequence's Z-transform ROC contains the unit circle, its DTFT equals X(z) evaluated at z=e^{jΩ}. The DTFT inherits linearity, time shift, multiplication by n, and convolution properties from the Z transform. [Session 18, slides 39–40]

An all-pass system can have unit magnitude at every frequency while substantially altering phase. For H(z)=(1−az)/(z−a), numerator and denominator become conjugate-length vectors on the unit circle, hence |H(e^{jΩ})|=1. [Session 18, slides 5–7]

Time reversal x[−n] maps DTFS coefficients a_k to a_{−k}; for real x[n], conjugate symmetry makes this equivalent to negating every spectral phase while preserving magnitude. Speech played backward demonstrates that phase carries temporal organization. [Session 18, slides 8–14]

In two-dimensional Fourier reconstruction, retaining phase while changing magnitude preserves recognizable object geometry far more strongly than retaining magnitude with uniform or unrelated phase. [Session 18, slides 41–47]

Parseval's CTFS identity is (1/T)∫_T|x(t)|²dt=Σ_k|a_k|². It follows by taking the zero coefficient of |x(t)|² and turns a lowpass cutoff choice into a sum of retained harmonic energies. [Problem Set 9, Problem 4 and solution]

For a periodic extension z(t)=Σ_kx(t+kT), convolution with a time-domain impulse train multiplies X(jω) by a frequency-domain impulse train. Periodic extension therefore samples the continuous spectrum; each spectral impulse has area 2π times its Fourier-series coefficient. [Session 19, slides 9–21]

Sampling x(t) every T seconds can be represented by multiplication with an impulse train. Frequency-domain convolution then repeats scaled copies of X(jω) every 2π/T, producing a periodic spectrum and exposing the mechanism behind aliasing. [Session 19, slides 25–33]

The CT transform of the impulse-sampled signal and the DTFT of its sample sequence have the same shape under Ω=ωT. Thus continuous frequency measured in rad/s maps to dimensionless discrete frequency modulo 2π. [Session 19, slides 30–33]

Periodic extension of a DT signal samples its already periodic DTFT, yielding a representation discrete and periodic in both time and frequency; the impulse weights are again 2π times the DTFS coefficients. [Session 19, slides 34–41]

The four representations form one structural table: periodicity in time implies discreteness in frequency, discreteness in time implies periodicity in frequency, and taking the period to infinity changes a series into a transform. [Session 19, slides 3–9 and 38–42]

A periodic LTI input/output pair is impossible if the proposed output has a nonzero harmonic where the input coefficient is zero, because filtering only multiplies corresponding coefficients. The reverse implication is only permissive: shared support means the pair could be LTI, not that it must be. [Problem Set 8, Problem 4 and solution]

Magnitude-only RC-like filtering attenuates upper square-wave harmonics symmetrically, while phase-only RC-like filtering preserves their sizes but shifts them toward peak alignment and can create a much larger overshoot. Magnitude controls harmonic strength; phase controls temporal alignment and asymmetry. [Problem Set 9, Problem 5 and solution]

For the ideal periodic DT lowpass H(e^{jΩ})=1 on |Ω|<π/2 and zero elsewhere, inverse transformation gives h[0]=1/2 and h[n]=sin(πn/2)/(πn) for n≠0. Applied to a period-3 impulse train, only its DC Fourier-series term passes, so y[n]=1/3. [Quiz 3, Problems 3–4 and solution]

For an echo h(t)=δ(t−T1)+fδ(t−T2), H(jω)=e^{−jωT1}[1+fe^{−jω(T2−T1)}]. Magnitude ripple spacing identifies T2−T1, ripple depth identifies f, and the average phase slope identifies T1. [Quiz 3, Problem 5 and solution]
pedagogy: A tightly sequenced, representation-comparison treatment. The lectures derive each Fourier representation from one already known—CTFT from CTFS as T→∞, DTFT from DTFS as N→∞, and both transforms from Laplace/Z restrictions—then repeatedly ask learners to move among waveform, coefficients, pole–zero geometry, magnitude, phase, and filtered output. ‘Check Yourself’ slides pose a visual classification or aliasing question before revealing the answer, while long animation sequences vary one vector, harmonic, or FFT block at a time. Physical audio examples, vowel recordings, speech reversal, images, speakers, and echoes precede or punctuate algebra. The three problem sets contain 21 multi-part problems, including engineering-design investigations of Gibbs/Fejér convergence, Parseval-based cutoff choice, and isolated magnitude/phase filtering; full solutions emphasize symmetry checks and alternative derivations. Homework 10 is ungraded review, and Quiz 3 is a two-hour, five-problem synthesis assessment spanning transforms, pole–zero response, DT inverse transforms, periodic filtering, and echo inference. Prerequisites are the earlier course treatment of complex exponentials, LTI systems, convolution, Laplace and Z transforms, poles/zeros, calculus, geometric sums, and basic Matlab/Python plotting.

gems: The square-versus-triangle comparison compresses a major regularity principle into one picture: the square's 1/k spectrum rings, the once-integrated triangle's 1/k² spectrum converges quickly, and both facts fall out of the differentiation property. [Session 14, slides 32–41]

Fourier's historical provocation is made concrete rather than ceremonial: continuous sinusoids sum to a discontinuous square wave, the very claim Lagrange mocked, and the persistent 9% edge overshoot explains why the paradox remains visible at every finite truncation. [Session 14, slides 18–20 and 39–41]

Instrument spectra turn consonance into arithmetic: notes whose fundamentals share a simple ratio align many harmonic lines, while inharmonic combinations collide without a common low-order pattern. [Session 14, slides 4–15]

The vowel sequence moves from waveform to spectrum to anatomy to singing. One glottal buzz filtered by different vocal-tract resonances explains formants, then high pitch removes enough harmonic samples that a sustained vowel becomes hard to identify. [Session 15, slides 11–35]

The limit from Fourier series to Fourier transform is animated as a sampling-density story: doubling the time period doubles the number of spectral samples in the same band until the line envelope becomes a continuum. [Session 16, slides 3–15]

The ideal lowpass pair is intentionally unsettling: a perfectly rectangular passband in frequency requires a two-sided sinc impulse response extending forever, linking sharp spectral walls to nonlocal time behavior. [Session 16, slides 29–32]

Sampling three CT cosines at T=0.001 s reverses their intuitive order: Ω=3,4,5 fold to effective cosine frequencies 3, about 2.283, and about 1.283 rad/sample, so the 5000-rad/s sinusoid becomes the lowest DT frequency. [Session 17, slides 31–42]

The DTFS has a rare finite-dimensional payoff: N time samples and exactly N roots-of-unity harmonics form inverse matrices, so the abstract series becomes ordinary linear algebra. [Session 17, slides 45–53]

The eight-point FFT derivation counts its own work: direct evaluation costs 64 multiplications, the first even/odd split costs 40, and recursive splitting yields Nlog₂N. The algorithm emerges from reused roots rather than appearing as a black box. [Session 18, slides 19–32]

Backward speech is introduced as a phase-only transformation: real-signal time reversal conjugates the spectrum, preserving every magnitude while negating every phase, yet intelligibility collapses. [Session 18, slides 8–14]

The harbor/mandrill experiment makes phase dominance visceral. Uniform magnitude plus the harbor's phase still exposes cranes and rigging, while the harbor magnitude with uniform phase becomes a nearly unrecognizable texture; swapping spectra follows the phase donor's geometry. [Session 18, slides 41–47]

A single four-quadrant chart unifies all Fourier cases: periodic↔discrete across the diagonal and discrete time↔periodic frequency down the columns, turning four formula sets into consequences of two structural switches. [Session 19, slides 3–9 and 38–42]

Periodic extension and sampling are presented as dual operations with the same impulse-train machinery: repeat in time to sample frequency; sample in time to repeat frequency. [Session 19, slides 9–33]

The sawtooth design problem goes beyond naming Gibbs: students estimate the limiting 1.09 peak and then discover that averaging partial sums removes it, an accessible empirical entrance to Fejér summation. [Problem Set 8, Problem 5 and solution]

The Parseval design problem converts a qualitative lowpass choice into a 90%-energy requirement for geometrically decaying coefficients α^{|k|}, then solves explicitly for the minimum retained harmonic index and cutoff. [Problem Set 9, Problem 4b and solution]

Separating an RC filter into magnitude-only and phase-only thought experiments produces opposite surprises: attenuation removes asymmetry, whereas phase delays without attenuation line up many upper harmonics into a large peak. [Problem Set 9, Problem 5 and solution]
Duality turns a potentially difficult integral into one line: once e^{−|t|}↔2/(1+ω²) is known, 1/(1+t²)↔πe^{−|ω|} follows by exchanging time and frequency. [Problem Set 10, Problem 4 and solution]

Quiz 3 treats an echo as parameter estimation rather than forward calculation: comb-ripple period reveals path-delay difference, ripple depth reveals echo strength f=0.2, and phase slope gives T1=π/1500 before T2=π/300 follows. [Quiz 3, Problem 5 and solution]
